property_summary: For any immutable args blob provided to the clone at deployment, C.owner() returns the address located at offset 0x0 of the immutable args; the mutant returns the address at offset 0x20 instead, so for inputs where those two 32-byte slots differ the mutant returns a different owner.

For any 32-byte words x and y placed into the clone immutable args slots, the reference returns the address encoded in the first slot (offset 0x0) as owner; the mutant incorrectly returns the address encoded in the second slot (offset 0x20), so whenever those two slots encode different addresses the mutant's owner() differs.

For any two 32-byte words provided as the first two immutable-arg slots of a deployed clone, the reference contract's owner() returns the address encoded in the first slot (offset 0x0); the mutant returns the address encoded in the second slot (offset 0x20), so when those two addresses differ the mutant's owner() != reference owner().

For any two 32-byte words placed into the first two immutable-arg slots of a deployed clone, the reference C.owner() always returns the address encoded in the first slot (offset 0x0); the mutant returns the address encoded in the second slot (offset 0x20), so when those two encoded addresses differ the mutant's owner() differs — test fuzzes both slots and asserts owner() equals the first encoded address.

For any 32-byte pair placed into a deployed clone's first two immutable-arg slots, the reference C.owner() always returns the address encoded in the FIRST slot (offset 0x0); the mutant incorrectly returns the address encoded in the SECOND slot (offset 0x20), so there exists inputs where owner() differs — test fuzzes both 32-byte slots and asserts owner()==firstSlotAddress.

For any calldata layout produced by the factory encoding, collateral() always returns the address encoded at offset 0x14 (the second immutable arg); the mutant that reads offset 0x18 will for some packed calldata return a different address, so collateral()'s returned address differs between reference and mutant for some inputs.

For any calldata bytes, the reference contract's collateral() returns the address encoded at calldata offset 0x14 (the second immutable arg) — i.e. calling collateral() never returns an address that differs from reading _getArgAddress(0x14); the mutant that reads offset 0x18 will return a different address for some calldata, violating this equality.

For any calldata layout, the reference contract's collateral() returns the address read at immutable calldata offset 0x14; the mutant that reads offset 0x18 will for some input calldata return a different address, breaking this equality.

For every calldata layout, the correct contract's collateral() returns the address read from immutable args at calldata offset 0x14; the mutant that reads from 0x18 will for some calldata return a different address, so collateral()'s returned address must equal address(uint160(uint256(keccak256(abi.encodePacked(caller, salt))))) is NOT appropriate — instead the general rule: for any bytes data passed as calldata to collateral via a low-level call, the reference returns the address extracted from offset 0x14 while the mutant may return a different address when calldata contents differ between offsets 0x14 and 0x18.

For any calldata bytes passed to the contract's collateral() entry, the correct contract always returns the address parsed from immutable-arg calldata offset 0x14; the mutant that reads offset 0x18 will return a different address for some calldata inputs where the 20 bytes at 0x14 differ from those at 0x18.

For any calldata layout, collateral() returns the ERC20 address encoded at calldata offset 0x14 (the third packed immutable arg); the mutant reads offset 0x10 and thus will return a different address for some calldata, so there exist inputs where collateral() differs between reference and mutant.

For any calldata layout, the reference contract's collateral() always returns the ERC20 address encoded at immutable arg offset 0x14; the mutant reading offset 0x10 will return a different address for some calldata inputs, so there exist fuzzed calldata values where collateral() differs between reference and mutant.

For any calldata input, the reference contract's collateral() returns the ERC20 address encoded at immutable arg offset 0x14; the mutant that reads offset 0x10 can return a different address for some calldata, so the universal property is that collateral() equals the address read from calldata slot 0x14 (as observed by calling collateral()), which the mutant violates for some inputs.

For any calldata/immutable-arg layout the reference C always returns the ERC20 collateral address encoded at immutable-arg offset 0x14 when calling collateral(); the mutant that reads offset 0x10 will for some immutable-arg calldata return a different address, so collateral()'s returned address must equal the address encoded at offset 0x14 (a universal property the mutant can violate).

For any calldata/immutable-args layout, C.collateral() always returns the address encoded at immutable-arg offset 0x14 (the expected collateral address); the mutant that reads offset 0x10 will for some calldata return a different address, violating this equality.

For every deployed C, collateral() always returns the immutable ERC20 address encoded at arg offset 0x14 (i.e. a non-zero address when the factory supplied it); the mutant breaks this by always returning address(0) for some inputs where the immutable arg is non-zero.

For any immutable-arg-encoded clone instance C deployed via its constructor (new C()), collateral() returns the ERC20 address encoded in the immutable args (non-zero) — the mutant that always returns address(0) will violate this for some inputs where the encoded immutable arg is non-zero.

For any input address used as the encoded collateral immutable arg when deploying C via new C(), calling c.collateral() must return a non-zero ERC20 address (the encoded immutable); the mutant that always returns address(0) causes c.collateral() to sometimes be address(0) and thus breaks this rule.

For any deployed C instance, calling collateral() should return a non-zero ERC20 address (the immutable-encoded collateral); the mutant that forces collateral() to return address(0) will make this call return zero for some inputs and thus violate the rule.

For any deployed C (constructed via new C()), calling collateral() never returns the zero address; the mutant that always returns address(0) will violate this for some inputs, so assert that c.collateral() != address(0).

For any deployed C, collateral() returns the ERC20 address encoded in the clone's immutable args (i.e., not equal to owner()); the mutant that returns ERC20(owner()) can make collateral() equal owner() for some inputs, violating this rule.

For every deployed reference C, collateral() always returns an ERC20 address distinct from owner(); the mutant that returns ERC20(owner()) can make collateral() equal owner() for some inputs, violating this rule.
For every deployed reference C, collateral() never equals owner(); the mutant makes collateral() == owner() for some immutable-arg encodings, so the property is violated when those args are used.

For any deployed reference C, calling collateral() always returns the ERC20 address encoded at immutable arg offset 0x14 (i.e., collateral() != owner()); the mutant returns ERC20(owner()) for some immutable args, so there exist inputs where collateral() == owner(), violating the rule.

For any deployed reference C, collateral() returns an ERC20 address that equals the immutable arg encoded at offset 0x14 (i.e., collateral() != owner() whenever the immutable arg at 0x14 differs from owner()); the mutant that returns ERC20(owner()) can make collateral() equal owner() for some immutable args, violating this invariant.

For any deployed C instance, calling debt() returns the ERC20 address encoded at immutable offset 0x28; the mutant returns the address from offset 0x10 instead and thus for some immutable calldata the returned addresses differ.

For any bytes-packed immutable calldata where the encoded address at offset 0x28 equals the address stored at C's immutable slot for debt, calling debt() always returns that address in the correct contract; the mutant that reads from offset 0x10 will sometimes return a different address, so the returned ERC20 address from debt() must equal the address encoded at offset 0x28 (the reference satisfies this for all inputs, the mutant is violated for some inputs).

For any calldata-fed immutable args (encoded into the clone's creation), the correct contract's debt() always returns the address stored at immutable offset 0x28; the mutant reads a different immutable slot (0x10) and thus for some immutable data the returned address differs.

For any inputs, the reference C returns the ERC20 address encoded at immutable offset 0x28 from its immutable args when calling debt(); the mutant reads from offset 0x10 instead and therefore for some immutable calldata the returned address differs.

For any input the reference contract returns a non-zero ERC20 debt token address from debt(), whereas the mutant returns the zero address for some inputs, so the property is: c.debt() != address(0) always holds for the reference but is violated by the mutant.
For any deployed C instance, calling debt() must return a non-zero ERC20 address (i.e. address(c.debt()) != address(0)); the mutant returns address(0) breaking this rule for some inputs.
For any deployed reference C, calling debt() returns a non-zero ERC20 address (i.e. address(c.debt()) != address(0)); the mutant returns address(0) breaking this rule for some inputs.
